q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1945 the British people elected a Labour government. The new Prime Minister was Clement Atlee, who promised to introduce the welfare state outlined in the Beveridge Report. In 1948, Aneurin (Nye) Bevan, the Minister for Health, led the establishment of the National Health Service.
o: Aneurin Bevan led the establishment of the National Health Service
William Beveridge led the establishment of the National Health Service

q.t: Which report provided the basis of the modern welfare state, and in which year was it published?
q.e: William Beveridge is best known for the 1942 report Social Insurance and Allied Services, known as the Beveridge Report. The report was commissioned by the wartime government in 1941. It provided the basis of the modern welfare state.

q.t: Which TWO of the five 'Giant Evils' named in the Beveridge Report are listed below?
q.e: It recommended that the government should find ways of fighting the five 'Giant Evils' of Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness and provided the basis of the modern welfare state.

q.t: What did the Education Act 1944, often called 'The Butler Act', introduce?
q.e: Richard Austen Butler oversaw the introduction of the Education Act 1944, often called 'The Butler Act', which introduced free secondary education in England and Wales. The division between primary and secondary schools that it enforced still remains in most areas of Britain.
o: Free secondary education in England and Wales
Free university education throughout the UK
Free school meals for all children

q.t: What phrase describes the protection the new system of benefits was intended to give?
q.e: A national system of benefits was also introduced to provide 'social security', so that the population would be protected from the 'cradle to the grave'.
o: From the cradle to the grave
From the workhouse to the grave

q.t: Which TWO industries were taken into public ownership by the post-war Labour government?
q.e: The government took into public ownership (nationalised) the railways, coal mines and gas, water and electricity supplies. Attlee's government undertook the nationalisation of major industries like coal and steel.

q.t: In 1947, independence was granted to how many countries?
q.e: Another aspect of change was self-government for former colonies. In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including India, Pakistan and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. Other colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific achieved independence over the next 20 years.

q.t: Which Prime Minister was famous for his 'wind of change' speech about decolonisation?
q.e: Britain had a Conservative government from 1951 to 1964. The Prime Minister of the day, Harold Macmillan, was famous for his 'wind of change' speech about decolonisation and independence for the countries of the Empire.

q.t: In 1948, people from which region were invited to come to the UK and work?
q.e: There were labour shortages and the British government encouraged workers from Ireland and other parts of Europe to come to the UK and help with the reconstruction. In 1948, people from the West Indies were also invited to come and work.

q.t: How many people of Indian origin forced to leave Uganda did Britain admit during the early 1970s?
q.e: The number of people migrating from the West Indies, India, Pakistan and what is now Bangladesh fell in the late 1960s because the government passed new laws to restrict immigration to Britain. Even so, during the early 1970s, Britain admitted 28,000 people of Indian origin who had been forced to leave Uganda.

q.t: Which TWO well-known pop music groups of the 1960s are named in the handbook?
q.e: The decade of the 1960s was a period of significant social change. It was known as 'the Swinging Sixties'. Two well-known pop music groups at the time were The Beatles and The Rolling Stones.

q.t: Which aircraft did Britain and France develop together?
q.e: The 1960s was also a time of technological progress. Britain and France developed the world's only supersonic commercial airliner, Concorde. It first flew in 1969 and began carrying passengers in 1976. Concorde was retired from service in 2003.

q.t: Who invented the cash-dispensing ATM, and where was the first one put into use?
q.e: In the 1960s, James Goodfellow invented the cash-dispensing ATM, automatic teller machine, or 'cashpoint'. The first of these was put into use by Barclays Bank in Enfield, north London in 1967.
o: James Goodfellow, and the first was at Barclays Bank in Enfield
Sir Christopher Cockerell, and the first was at Barclays Bank in Enfield
James Goodfellow, and the first was at the Bank of England
Sir Frank Whittle, and the first was in Glasgow

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Radar was developed by Scotsman Sir Robert Watson-Watt, who proposed that enemy aircraft could be detected by radio waves. The jet engine was developed in Britain in the 1930s by Sir Frank Whittle, a British Royal Air Force engineer officer.
o: Sir Frank Whittle developed the jet engine
Sir Robert Watson-Watt developed the jet engine

q.t: Where was the radio telescope built by Sir Bernard Lovell?
q.e: Working with radar led Sir Bernard Lovell to make new discoveries in astronomy. The radio telescope he built at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire was for many years the biggest in the world and continues to operate today.

q.t: Who invented the hovercraft, and in which decade?
q.e: Sir Christopher Cockerell, a British inventor, invented the hovercraft in the 1950s.

q.t: Which TWO scientists led the team that first cloned a mammal in 1996?
q.e: In 1996, two British scientists, Sir Ian Wilmot and Keith Campbell, led a team which was the first to succeed in cloning a mammal, Dolly the sheep.

q.t: On what date was information successfully transferred via the World Wide Web for the first time?
q.e: The inventor of the World Wide Web, Sir Tim Berners-Lee, is British. Information was successfully transferred via the web for the first time on 25 December 1990.

q.t: Where was the world's first 'test-tube baby' born, and in which year?
q.e: IVF, in-vitro fertilisation, therapy for the treatment of infertility was pioneered in Britain by physiologist Sir Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe. The world's first 'test-tube baby' was born in Oldham, Lancashire in 1978.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1972, the Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended and Northern Ireland was directly ruled by the UK government. Some 3,000 people lost their lives in the decades after 1969 in the violence in Northern Ireland.
o: The Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended in 1972
The Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended in 1969

q.t: For what did Mary Peters win an Olympic gold medal in 1972?
q.e: Born in Manchester, Mary Peters moved to Northern Ireland as a child. She was a talented athlete who won an Olympic gold medal in the pentathlon in 1972. She was made a Dame of the British Empire in 2000.

q.t: Which islands did Argentina invade in 1982?
q.e: In 1982, Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic. A naval taskforce was sent from the UK and military action led to the recovery of the islands.

q.t: Which Prime Minister followed Margaret Thatcher and helped establish the Northern Ireland peace process?
q.e: Margaret Thatcher led the Conservative government from 1979 to 1990. John Major was Prime Minister after Mrs Thatcher, and helped establish the Northern Ireland peace process.

q.t: Roald Dahl was born in Wales to parents of which nationality?
q.e: Roald Dahl was born in Wales to Norwegian parents. He served in the Royal Air Force during the Second World War. His best-known works include Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and George's Marvellous Medicine.
